full_text:
Note: This interview is not transcribed, but based on notes taken by interviewer.

No previous experience of the industry, and neither parent is in engineering industry.
On the BSc in Construction Management Course at [name] University.
Applied to architecture course after ‘A’ levels in Art and Psychology, but didn’t get in.  So went on Foundation course in Built Environment at [same university].
This got Clare interested in becoming a project manager, and building houses etc.  Also a well paid job.
Didn’t have any careers advice at school.
Decided to do construction management at [name] University because it was a bit unusual and far away from her parents.
Didn’t decide to do a placement until she got to university.

Thought that engineering would be male-dominated, but not a concern at university.  Is concerned, however, that she won’t be taken seriously in the workplace.

Thinks that more women should be encouraged to do engineering and that this could possibly be done by providing more information to girls at school.

Thinks that a good engineer needs to be a born leader and confident – characteristics that are usually perceived as male.

Thinks that the main disadvantage of being a female engineer is that men might not take you seriously.

Has enjoyed the course so far.  Thinks that the best thing is improved confidence with working with the guys.  But worst bit is only 1 other girl on course (who isn’t doing placement, so will be only girl in final year).

Has been taught by one female lecturer but would be encouraging to be taught by more especially if they had good degree etc.
Some male lecturers don’t necessarily treat you differently, but do act differently around you.  For example, making comments or swearing, and then apologising.
No personal tutor.
Greatest influence probably [male lecturer], another lecturer and a fellow student, who are all very encouraging.

Have to do lots of group work as part of course.  Get put into groups – don’t usually have a choice of who to work with.  Thinks that men and women do bring different skills to group work, e.g. women more organised, but men don’t always take you seriously.
No really good or bad experiences of group work, but thinks experience will help in industry.

University has helped prepare students for placement with two weeks of classes covering things like what to expect from placement, writing CVs, interviews etc.  Would also be encouraging to have a woman from industry to come and talk to female students about their experiences.

Principal reason for choosing to go on placement was because she had no experience in industry and thought that when applying for jobs, this would count more than anything else.  [Male lecturer] and boyfriend also encouraged her to go on placement.  Also thought that work experience would be particularly helpful in being a woman.

Other students in class that are not going on placement are doing so because they already have experience, they are part-time students, or because they are not that bothered about degree, or can’t see far enough ahead to see how it will benefit them.

Is going on placement with [company].  Was attracted to this company because they are interested in increasing number of women working for them and because they do project management work.
She did some research into the company on the internet when she found out she had an interview.  The university found this placement for her, via [male lecturer/placement co-ordinator].

Is not expecting to find that she will put theory into practice on placement.  Has been told that everything she’s learnt will go out the window when on placement.  However, does think that it will improve confidence and will help with assignments in the final year.

Thinks the best thing about placement will be getting paid and improving confidence working with men.  Most apprehensive about first two weeks of work and not being taken seriously on site, especially by labourers.  Doesn’t think that you can prepare for this, just learn not to take it too seriously.  While she thought that all students may experience this to some extent, she thought it would be worse as a woman.   She did, however, think this would improve as everyone got to know her and realised that she did know what she was talking about, and so on.
Has heard that this does happen on placements.

Thought that work would mainly differ from uni in that you would have to use your initiative a lot more and ask for help if you need it, whereas at uni you are just given it.

Thought that in 5 years time would hopefully be a good project manager earning lots of money, and have a husband, house and nice car.
Above would be ideal career, or possibly being executive of own company.  Would like to work abroad because it is too cold here!  Although career prospects are ok here, would love to work in Australia where career prospects are good as there is a shortage of professionals.

Would describe the engineering industry as hard-working, demanding and masculine.  It is masculine mainly because of the number of men, but also because the type of work is seen as masculine.  Thought that the situation would improve for women but could be slow process, but has moved on a lot in last 10 years, so why not in next 10?

Happy with all career choices.  Thinks it fate that she didn’t do well in ‘A’ levels, or wouldn’t have gone through clearing, foundation course, and course she’s on now, which she really enjoys.

Did originally enrol for QS course (and was only girl on course) but didn’t get on with teacher.  In first lesson the male lecturer asked her to clean the board, to which she asked, why are you asking me, because I’m a woman?  After that had loads on women jokes, which she didn’t find offensive, just not funny.  Also he was poor teacher and QS was boring course – so transferred to construction management.
